title: Engineering of Chirped Apodized Sources for Quantum Spectroscopy
authors: Linda Sansoni, Max Widarsson, Patrick Mutter, Andrea Chiuri
abstract: Quantum sources of light are of paramount importance for the development of photonic quantum technologies. The growing demand for bright, efficient, and spectrally engineered photonic sources for applications in quantum sensing, spectroscopy, and imaging has motivated the development of tailored nonlinear crystals. Here, we report on the development and characterization of chirped, apodized KTP crystals specifically engineered for quantum spectroscopy. Our source exhibits an unprecedented bandwidth in a highly non-degenerate configuration, demonstrating its potential to support quantum spectroscopy protocols over broad spectral ranges while enabling significantly shorter measurement times.
summary: This paper details the engineering of chirped and apodized nonlinear crystals, such as KTP, to create superior quantum light sources. By tailoring the crystal's nonlinear profile, the authors achieve unprecedented broadband emission while suppressing spectral ripples. This advancement provides a powerful tool for next-generation quantum spectroscopy and sensing applications.
main_problem: The core problem is developing highly efficient, spectrally engineered, and bright quantum light sources necessary for advanced quantum sensing and spectroscopy applications.
main_result: The authors report that engineering chirped and apodized nonlinear crystals (caKTP) successfully generates broadband, flat-spectrum correlated photon pairs, enabling quantum spectroscopy over wide spectral ranges with shorter measurement times.
method: The methodology involves theoretical simulation and experimental characterization of nonlinear processes like SPDC using tailored crystal geometries (chirping and apodization) to control the spectral output.
model_or_system: The physical system is the nonlinear crystal, specifically KTP, which is engineered with a chirped and apodized nonlinear coefficient profile. The process relies on Type-0 Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC) to generate correlated photon pairs.
key_observables: Broad spectral bandwidth, flat intensity distribution, high pair generation rate, and preservation of quantum correlations.
important_parameters: Nonlinear crystal length (e.g., 2 mm vs 30 mm), pump wavelength (e.g., 532 nm), and the degree of chirp/apodization.
main_assumptions: The work assumes the ability to implement precise nonlinear coefficient engineering (chirping/apodization) and operates under conditions where quantum correlations are maintained despite high count rates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the effect of nonlinear-chirp apodization on phase-matching spectra, showing broadband visible-MIR generation, and detail the experimental setup for source characterization.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the need for engineered quantum sources, detailing the theoretical basis of nonlinear-chirp apodization, presenting simulation results demonstrating bandwidth enhancement, and concluding with the practical advantages for quantum spectroscopy.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems, as it details the engineering of quantum light sources—a crucial resource for quantum information processing and sensing protocols.

The black dotted line indicates the transition from linear chirp to apodization. (b) Corresponding phase-matching spectra. (c) Poling- period profile for the 30 mm crystal. The black dotted line indicates the transition from linear chirp to apodization. (d) Corresponding phase-matching spectra.

Figure 2: Simulated spectrum of a 2 mm-long nonlinear-chirp-apodized ppKTP crystal pumped at 532 nm. The nominal poling period varies from 12.38 µm to 13.71 µm, and the resulting idler spectrum extends from approximately 2.6 µm to 3.6 µm.

Figure 3: Experimental Setup for characterization of the chirped apodized source. Here a pulsed laser at 532 nm (8 ps pulses with PRR=40 MHz) impinges on the caKTP crystal. Pairs of single photons in the VIS and IR range are produced and split on a dichroic mirror (DM). The IR photon goes through a target sample (T) and is then detected by a single pixel SPAD; the VIS photon is spectrally analyzed by means of a spectrograph (S) and an intensified CCD camera (iCCD). Coincidences between the detector and the camera are recorded (&).

Figure 4: (a) Spectrum of a 2mm-long caKTP. The blue curve reports the correlated spectrum, while the orange dashed line refers to the uncorrelated measurements where the background - counts when the SPDC source is blocked - has been subtracted. The reduced spectral width of the correlated spectrum is due to limited detection efficiency of the telecom detector for wavelengths above 1600 nm. (b) Correlated spectra of 1mm- (red curve) and 2mm-long crystals (blue curve). It is clear that the longer the crystal, the broader the spectrum.
